segments.text: Welcome to video five of our Jira for
Scrum tutorial series. In this video, we
will learn how to create and manage a
product backlog in Jira. The product
backlog is one of the most important
Scrum artifacts because it contains the
work that may be required to deliver and
improve the product. We will learn how
to add user stories and tasks, write
effective backlog items, prioritize
them, and keep the backlog organized and
ready for sprint planning. Let's start
with the product backlog. In Scrum, the
product backlog is an ordered list of
everything that may be needed to improve
the product. In Jira, these backlog
items are represented as issues. The
backlog can contain different types of
work, including user stories, tasks,
bugs, technical improvements, and
research activities. An important point
is that the backlog is not simply a long
to-do list. It should be continuously
refined, clarified, and ordered based on
product value, risk, dependencies, and
other considerations. In Jira, you can
access the product backlog from your
Scrum project by selecting the backlog
option. Here, we can see our backlog
items, their issue types, and their
relative order. The product owner and
Scrum team can use this view to
understand what work is coming up and
decide which items should be considered
for upcoming sprints. Notice that the
backlog can contain different types of
issues, not just user stories. Now,
let's create our first user story. We
can select create and choose the story
issue type. For the summary, we could
write user can reset a forgotten
password. In the description, we can use
the classic user story format. As a
registered user, I want to reset my
forgotten password so that I can regain
access to my account.
This format helps the team understand
who needs the functionality, what they
need, and why they need it. A good
backlog item should be clear, valuable,
understandable, and testable. It should
also be small enough for the team to
understand and potentially complete
within a sprint. Compare these two
examples. Build authentication system is
very broad. User can log in using email
and password is much more specific. The
second item gives the team a clearer
understanding of the expected
functionality and can be further refined
with acceptance criteria. Not every
backlog item needs to be written as a
user story. Some work is better
represented as a task. For example,
configuring password encryption may be
technical work that supports a user
story. We can create a task in Jira and
provide a clear summary and description.
The important principle is that the
issue should communicate the work
clearly to the team. The backlog may
also contain defects or bugs. For
example, suppose a user requests a
password reset but does not receive the
email. We can create a bug issue and
provide useful information such as the
steps to reproduce the problem, the
expected result, the actual result, and
the environment where the problem
occurred. This information helps
developers understand and resolve the
defect efficiently. Creating backlog
items is only the first step. We also
need to order them. In Scrum, the
product backlog is an ordered list. The
items near the top generally represent
work that should be considered sooner.
For example, user login may have higher
priority than theme customization
because login is essential to using the
application.
In Jira, we can change the order of
backlog items by moving them up or down
in the backlog. How should we decide
what comes first?
Prioritization should consider multiple
factors.
Business and customer value are
important, but they are not the only
considerations. We should also consider
risk, dependencies, urgency, and the
effort required. For example, a
technically difficult item may need to
be addressed early if it represents a
significant technical risk or blocks
several other features. Product backlog
items are not fixed forever. As the team
learns more about the product,
customers, and technology, backlog items
may need to change. In Jira, we can edit
the summary, description, priority,
labels, assignee, story points, and
other fields. This continuous refinement
helps keep the backlog relevant and
useful. A healthy product backlog should
be organized. Items near the top should
generally be better understood and
closer to being ready for sprint
planning. Items further down may require
more clarification or may represent
future possibilities. The team should
regularly review and refine the backlog
instead of allowing it to become an
unmanageable collection of old and
unclear items. Backlog management is an
ongoing activity. During backlog
refinement, the product owner and Scrum
team review upcoming items, clarify
requirements, split large items, add
acceptance criteria, estimate the work,
and reorder items when necessary. The
objective is to make the most important
upcoming work sufficiently understood
and ready for sprint planning. Let's
look at a simple example. Imagine that
we are developing an e-commerce
application. Our backlog might contain
user login, product search, shopping
cart functionality, a payment defect,
and database optimization work. We can
order these items based on their value,
urgency, dependencies, and risk. As the
product evolves, we can continuously add
new items, modify existing items, and
change their order. Let's summarize what
we learned.
The product backlog is an ordered list
of work required to improve the product.
Jira allows us to create and manage
different types of backlog items,
including user stories, tasks, and bugs.
Good backlog items should be clear,
valuable, understandable, and testable.
Most importantly, the backlog should be
continuously refined and reordered as we
learn more about the product.
In the next video, we will move from
backlog management to sprint planning in
Jira, where we will learn how backlog
items are selected for a sprint.
